newsitem.title: USA: Key Democrat see close vote on U.S. trade measure.
newsitem.headline: Key Democrat see close vote on U.S. trade measure.

text.p: A leading House Democrat said Tuesday he expected a major battle in Congress over trade negotiation legislation and said any vote would be close.

House Minority Whip David Bonior, a Michigan Democrat, said he and labour and environmental groups who oppose expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement in its present form will be working hard over the next few months to fight legislation that would give the White House authority to negotiate new trade agreements.
"We are going to work hard in the months ahead to make sure the American people know about the effects of NAFTA," Bonior to a NAFTA conference.

He said the results of NAFTA, which joins the United States, Canada and Mexico in a trade zone, have fallen short of the promises made by supporters. Nearly four years after NAFTA passed Congress the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico stands at $16 billion, he said.

About 1,400 U.S. factories have shut down or moved out of the United States or downsized as a result of NAFTA, and real wages for Mexico have fallen by about 40 percent, Bonior said. He said the deficit in automobile trade is up sharply and that Mexico now ships more cars to the United States, than are shipped out of the United States to the rest of the world.

Those observations coupled with concerns about drugs crossing the border into the United States and health concerned raised by an outbreak of hepatitis-A among schoolchildren who had eaten tainted strawberries grown in Mexico, underscore the difficulty the White House faces in winning new trade negotiation authority from Congress.

Bonior said some preliminary pulse-taking in Congress has been encouraging and said some Democrats who voted for NAFTA four years ago may vote differently when the so-called fast trade trade negotiation legislation gets to Congress.
"We expect this to be a very, very tight vote, as tight as the NAFTA vote was 40 months ago," he said.
Administration officials have been working behind the scenes to try to form a consensus on so-called fast-track legislation.

The bill would allow U.S. trade officials to negotiate an expansion of NAFTA to include Chile and other trade agreements without fear they will later be changed by Congress, which could either accept or reject an agreement in its entirety without making individual changes.

A dispute over whether labour and environment issues should be included in the legislation has delayed it. The administration and its key Democratic supporters want labour and environment issues included, but Republicans who control Congress want a narrower trade negotiation authority.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky has scheduled several visits this week with key lawmakers in an effort to forge legislation that will win bipartisan support, a spokesman for the trade representative said.
